title: 'Miracle on the Hudson' Pilot Sully Sullenberger Reveals Early-Stage Alzheimer's Diagnosis
excerpt: The 75-year-old hero who saved 155 lives by landing a crippled jet on the Hudson River says he will use his platform to raise awareness and give hope to millions of families living with the disease
body:
Captain Chesley "Sully" Sullenberger III, the airline pilot who became an international hero after safely landing US Airways Flight 1549 on New York's Hudson River in 2009, revealed on Tuesday that he has been diagnosed with early-stage Alzheimer's disease.

Sullenberger, now 75, disclosed the diagnosis in a statement on his website and in an interview with PEOPLE magazine, saying he received the news in August 2025 after noticing he was forgetting things.

"It is early stage. For now, this means a name may not come easily to me, I forget a story I have recently told, or I don't sleep as well," Sullenberger said, "but I am in the beginning of this long journey."

## A Lifetime of Service

The Danville, California resident spent 30 years as a commercial airline pilot after serving as a U.S. Air Force fighter pilot. His life took a dramatic turn on January 15, 2009, when a flock of Canada geese struck both engines of his Airbus A320 shortly after takeoff from New York's LaGuardia Airport.

With both engines destroyed and no airport within reach, Sullenberger made the split-second decision to ditch the aircraft in the Hudson River. All 155 passengers and crew survived in what became known worldwide as the "Miracle on the Hudson."

His composure under unimaginable pressure — captured in the iconic images of passengers standing on the plane's wings as ferry boats rushed to rescue them — made him a global symbol of courage and professionalism. The story was immortalized in the 2016 film "Sully," directed by Clint Eastwood and starring Tom Hanks.

## Using His Voice for Others

Sullenberger said he views the diagnosis not as an ending but as a new form of service. After decades of advocating for aviation safety — including fighting for increased pilot training, rest requirements, and the two-pilot rule — he now intends to use his platform for Alzheimer's awareness.

"This new phase of my life has challenged what it means to be of service. And the answer is to speak up," he said. "It is my hope that by sharing this, other families living in the shadows with this disease will feel they too can step forward."

His wife of 37 years, Lorrie Sullenberger, said the couple is navigating the diagnosis with "hope" and "joy." She added that Sully remains the same steady person he has always been — before and after Flight 1549, and before and after this diagnosis.

## A Legacy Beyond the Hudson

After retiring from flying in 2010, Sullenberger remained active in public life. He testified before Congress in 2019, urging lawmakers to require simulator training before Boeing 737 MAX flights could resume following two fatal crashes. "Our current system of aircraft design and certification has failed us," he told legislators.

He was inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in September 2025, the same month he received his Alzheimer's diagnosis. In 2022, he served as the U.S. Ambassador to the International Civil Aviation Organization, where he raised concerns about attempts to reduce pilot training requirements.

## The Scale of Alzheimer's

Sullenberger's announcement puts a well-known face on a disease that affects millions worldwide. According to the Alzheimer's Association, more than 6.9 million Americans aged 65 and older are living with the disease, and that number is projected to nearly double by 2050. There is currently no cure, though treatments are improving with early detection and new medications.

Sullenberger's doctor, Gil Rabinovici of UCSF Medical Center, noted that the disease "spares no age group and impacts millions of people around the world."

"Though it may impact my memory of the past, this diagnosis will not prevent me from looking forward to and appreciating our future," Sullenberger said. "So many people told us after Flight 1549 that the outcome gave them hope. Lorrie says we can all use a little of that hope right now."

Invoking the spirit that carried everyone to safety that freezing January afternoon 17 years ago, Sullenberger concluded: "I would say that courage can be contagious. Now we need that courage to battle this disease."

*Sources: Reuters, PEOPLE, USA Today, CNN*
